query: For a CoCrFeNi high-entropy-alloy matrix evaluated in sliding from room temperature to 800 °C, what single intervention could overcome the difficulty of maintaining low coefficient of friction and wear rate throughout the full temperature range? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains the mechanism expected to operate across the test regime, predicts performance relative to the starting CoCrFeNi material, specifies relevant temperature, load, and environmental boundaries, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes a controlled falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a minor amount of yttrium (around 1–2 at%) to the CoCrFeNi high‐entropy alloy matrix will promote the in situ formation of a stable, lubricious Y‐rich oxide tribolayer during sliding that remains effective from room temperature up to 800 °C, thereby maintaining a low coefficient of friction and reduced wear rate throughout the full temperature range.
generation.material_initial_state: CoCrFeNi high‐entropy alloy matrix with conventional composition (without yttrium addition), exhibiting typical friction and wear behavior that worsens at high temperatures.
generation.intervention: Alloy modification by doping the matrix with ~1–2 at% yttrium.
generation.conditions: Sliding wear tests conducted in dry air over a temperature range from room temperature (approximately 300 K) to 800 °C (approximately 1073 K) under a constant applied load typical of tribological testing.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a continuous, adherent, Y‐rich oxide layer (tribolayer) on the worn surface.
generation.mechanism: The yttrium addition promotes the nucleation and growth of thermodynamically stable, lubricious Y‐rich oxides during sliding. At elevated temperatures the Y‐rich oxide layer forms rapidly and remains intact, preventing direct metal–metal contact and reducing friction and wear. At lower temperatures, the alloy microstructure is minimally disturbed so that baseline mechanical properties are preserved.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the baseline CoCrFeNi alloy, the yttrium-doped alloy will exhibit a consistently lower coefficient of friction and a reduced wear rate across the entire temperature range (room temperature to 800 °C), due to the protective and lubricious behavior of the self-forming oxide tribolayer.
generation.baseline: CoCrFeNi high‐entropy alloy without yttrium addition, which shows increasing friction and wear rates at temperatures approaching 800 °C due to oxide instability or altered wear mechanisms.
generation.boundary: The intervention is expected to be effective in sliding conditions in dry air up to 800 °C; performance outside this temperature range or in different environmental atmospheres (e.g., high humidity or corrosive environments) is untested.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal yttrium concentration and the exact nature (thickness, continuity, composition) of the formed oxide layer may vary with processing conditions. Additionally, potential side effects on mechanical properties (such as strength or ductility) are uncertain and require further investigation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one set of the baseline CoCrFeNi alloy and one set doped with 1–2 at% yttrium under identical processing conditions. Conduct sliding wear tests in air over a temperature ramp from room temperature to 800 °C while measuring the coefficient of friction and wear rate. Post-test surface analysis (e.g., XPS, SEM, TEM) will be used to characterize the tribolayer formation and composition.
measurements: Wear rate (e.g., volumetric loss) versus temperature
Surface oxide layer composition and continuity via spectroscopic and microscopic analysis
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the yttrium-doped samples do not demonstrate a statistically significant reduction in friction coefficient and wear rate across the full temperature range relative to the baseline samples, and if no continuous Y-rich oxide tribolayer is observed on the worn surfaces, then the hypothesis is rejected.
